newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai election race too close to call - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Thai election race too close to call - analysts.

text.p: The two key parties contesting Sunday's Thai election, dubbed the dirtiest and most violent in two decades, are running such a tight race that an outcome is hard to predict, analysts said on Thursday.

The Democrat Party, led by former premier Chuan Leekpai, and the New Aspiration Party (NAP) of Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh are locked in a close battle for the most seats in the 393-seat parliament.

The winner will have the right to form a new coalition government to run the country, which has this year been hit by a sudden economic slowdown, sluggish exports and a ballooning current account deficit.
No single party has ever won a majority in previous elections enabling it to form an administration by itself.
"I believe that this race is very close and it will be difficult to predict the result," said Suchit Bunbongkarn, dean of political science at Chulalongkorn University.
A total of 2,310 candidates from 13 parties are contesting the election, the country's second in 16 months after premier Banharn Silpa-archa called snap polls in late September.

"The winner will make it by five to 10 seats. Thailand is facing a crisis of confidence among investors and whoever wins must restore confidence," said Pisarn Manoleehagul, president of the Thai Farmers Research Centre Co Ltd.
However, the respected Rajabhat Institute for teacher training, in its widely watched opinion poll on Thursday tipped the Democrats to win 149 seats and the NAP to come in second with 114 seats.

Analysts also noted that the Chart Pattana Party, led by former premier Chatchai Choonhavan and which now has 53 seats, was set to win the same number of seats and be the key party dictating the formation of a new coalition.

"Even if the NAP or Democrats win the most seats, the Chart Pattana will have the trump card. They will be needed by both to form a new coalition government," said Thammasat University political scientist Somjai Phagaphasvivat.

Most other private polls have had the two top contenders running neck and neck. The Krungthep Thurakij newspaper cited a private police Special Branch survey as saying the two parties would win 125 seats each.
Billions of baht have been spent by politicians in this election, marred by the killing of at least seven political workers by gunmen, according to police.
Thai Farmers Research Centre estimates 20 billion baht ($785.8 million) would be spent by politicians on this election, 20 percent more than the amount spent on the last polls 16 months ago.
Rajabhat Institute said this election campaign was the most violent and the dirtiest since the mid-1970s when student-led democracy groups toppled Thai military governments.

Pollwatch, the election watchdog, estimated that up to 30 billion baht had been spent, including on vote-buying. Some candidates handed out 100-baht notes to voters which could be exchanged for 200-baht notes if the candidates won.

Thai business is hoping the Democrats will win because they are seen as having a strong economic team, including a former finance minister. The NAP was seen as a party comprising many defectors from other parties and lack of cohesion would make managing the national economy difficult.

Analysts said the Democrats needed to win at least 25 of the 37 seats in Bangkok to ensure an election victory. This was because they were expected to win almost the same number of seats as the NAP in rural areas but a big win in Bangkok, where the NAP was not influential, could swing the balance. ($1=25.45 baht)
